text: We start with five, two, nine, one, six.
caption: We start with 5, 2, 9, 1, 6

text: Insertion sort works the way you sort a hand of cards.
On its own, the first card is already a sorted hand.
We will count every comparison and every shift along the way.
Pick up the next card, two, leaving a hole behind it.
Compare two with five: five is bigger, so five has to move.
Five shifts one place right, sliding into the hole.
Nothing is left of the hole, so two drops in at the front.
Pick up the next card, nine, from index two.
Compare nine with five: five is smaller, so we stop right away.
Nine drops straight back into the hole it came from.
Pick up the next card, one, opening a hole at index three.
Compare one with nine: nine is bigger, so nine has to move.
Nine shifts right, and the hole moves left to index two.
Compare one with five: five is bigger too, so five must move.
Five shifts right, and the hole moves left to index one.
Compare one with two: two is bigger as well, so it moves.
Two shifts right, and the hole reaches the very front.
Nothing is left to compare, so one drops in at index zero.
Pick up the last card, six, leaving a hole at index four.
Compare six with nine: nine is bigger, so nine has to move.
Nine shifts right into the hole, which moves to index three.
Compare six with five: five is smaller, so the search stops here.
Six drops into index three, between five and nine.
Every card is now in place: one, two, five, six, nine.
caption: Every card is now in place: 1, 2, 5, 6, 9

text: That took seven comparisons and five shifts for five cards.
A reversed array would force every card all the way left.
In general, the comparisons grow like n squared in the worst case.
But on nearly sorted input, each card stops after one comparison.
Pick up, shift the bigger cards right, and drop into the hole.
